Mechanism: P. vivax and P. ovale form hypnozoites in the liver, which can reactivate later. Primaquine is the only drug that clears liver hypnozoites, preventing relapse. Other options: Mefloquine -> used for prophylaxis and treatment, but does not eradicate liver hypnozoites. Proguanil -> prophylactic, not for relapse. Artemether -> effective for blood-stage parasites, not liver-stage hypnozoites.

Early presentation: Gastrointestinal symptoms, especially sudden vomiting, can occur within hours. Respiratory arrest and paralysis: Occur later if toxin affects neuromuscular junction; since the question specifies no paralysis, these are not included. Diarrhea and abdominal pain: May occur but vomiting is more characteristic of acute foodborne botulism. Key point: Projectile vomiting is an early hallmark of foodborne Clostridium botulinum intoxication. Reference: Robbins & Cotran, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Chapter on Bacterial Food Poisoning.
